a.basis: F156, F39: DNA's elevation triggers evaluation of non-adopting forensic occupations

b.basis: F88, F98, F102, F103, F152, F161; actual non-DNA reporting change
b.reason: Toxicology provides the paper’s documented instance of a neighboring nonadopting unit actually changing its local reporting practice because of the comparison.

a.basis: F39, F56: the NAS-driven evaluative tensions are what travel along the pathways
a.reason: C03's account has pathways carry and route the evaluation of neighboring occupations, so it takes C02's outcome, scrutiny drawn toward neighbors by DNA's benchmark status, as the input to the process, and nothing else in the paper supplies that input.

b.basis: F105, F129, F132, F153, F162; nonurgent professional debate and resistance
b.reason: The internal narcotics debate and continued crystal testing provide one of the contrasting routes through which C03 links urgency to local change.

a.basis: F39, F154: compatibility judged against DNA as benchmark
a.reason: Technical compatibility in C04 is compatibility with a benchmark imposed through comparison, which presupposes C02's outcome.

a.basis: F85, F86, F145: no workable firearms analogue to DNA's population statistics
a.reason: Firearms is the case of an incompatible technique making adaptation seem unworkable, one of the three cases behind C04.

b.basis: F64, F85–F87, F145, F151; firearms method incompatibility
b.reason: Firearms’ inability to translate DNA population statistics into microscopic-mark comparison is one instance of how technical mismatch limits feasible local adaptation.

a.basis: F100, F101, F146: measurement uncertainty fit toxicology's instrumented method
a.reason: Toxicology is the case where a compatible technique made adaptation straightforward, one of the cases from which C04 is drawn alongside firearms and narcotics.

b.basis: F91, F93, F98–F101, F146; toxicology fit and adaptation
b.reason: The toxicology reporting change offers an instance of technically feasible adaptation, alongside contrasting firearms and narcotics techniques.

a.basis: F147, F153, F166: compatible GC/MS option yet no change
a.reason: Narcotics is the only case showing that compatible technique does not by itself bring change, so nothing else supports C04's qualifying clause.

b.basis: F106, F108–F109, F126–F129, F147, F150, F153; compatible option without adoption
b.reason: Narcotics is the decisive case showing that the availability of a DNA-compatible instrumented method does not by itself produce local adaptation.

a.basis: F39, F56: DNA-centered evaluation is what values filter
a.reason: C05's process has values filtering an evaluative comparison, which takes C02's outcome, scrutiny drawn toward neighbors by DNA's benchmark status, as its input.

b.basis: F39, F56, F87, F100, F129; legitimacy comparison reaching occupational values
b.reason: The values-based response process requires some evaluative challenge from the legitimized DNA comparator to encounter and filter, which C02 supplies before differences in occupational values shape responses.

a.basis: F86, F87, F148: DNA-like objectivity affronted holistic subjective judgment
a.reason: Firearms is a case of value threat promoting resistance, though narcotics also supports that side of C05.

b.basis: F70, F77, F85–F87, F148, F151; value conflict and resistance

a.basis: F126-F129, F150: instrumentation threatened valued autonomy and variety, so analysts resisted

a.basis: F45-F47: DNA's statistics, error reporting and reviewable instrument output

b.basis: F45–F52, F85, F100, F106, F157; distinct DNA attributes available

a.reason: Firearms' reading of DNA as overarching statistical objectivity is one of the three instances showing different features selected.

b.basis: F85–F87, F145, F148, F157; statistical features selected
b.reason: Firearms examiners interpreted DNA principally through statistical objectivity, contributing one of the three specific interpretations underpinning C13.

a.basis: F157: toxicologists read DNA as measurement-error practice

b.basis: F89–F100, F146, F149, F157; error measurement singled out
b.reason: Toxicologists singled out error measurement rather than DNA identification as the pertinent comparison, one of the three selective interpretations.

a.reason: Narcotics' focus on DNA's instrumental output is one of the three instances showing that occupations select different features of the benchmark.

b.basis: F106, F121–F129, F147, F150, F157; instrument output foregrounded
b.reason: Narcotics emphasized instrument output and retrospective verifiability, a distinct reading of DNA alongside firearms’ statistics and toxicology’s measurement error.

a.reason: C20 stays supported by the unit descriptions, but part of its point is to explain why technique, alongside values, shapes responses, and C05 also carries that point.

b.reason: That a method is more or less compatible with DNA is different from the finding that occupational values arise within methods, which has its own observed basis (pp. 633, 637).

a.basis: Discussion offers intertwinement as why groups read new technology through their values and techniques
a.reason: C20's support, the descriptions of each unit's work and values, stands without C05, but the paper offers the intertwining to explain why responses run through values, and that point lapses if values do not filter the comparison.

b.reason: The paper derives C20 from how methods give rise to occupational commitments, not from the separate proposition that commitments predict adaptation or resistance (p. 637).

a.basis: F27, F58: distinct analytic work produced distinct cultures; text then notes values and technique intertwined

b.basis: F27, F58, F70, F97, F111; distinct work-generated cultures

a.basis: F75-F77: firearms judgment values built through training on best known non-matches
a.reason: Firearms examiners' value of holistic trained judgment arising from their comparative-microscopy training is one instance of values rooted in technique.

b.basis: F64, F69–F77, F86–F87, F148, F166; trained visual judgment
b.reason: Firearms’ microscopical judgments and commitment to holistic expertise are a concrete instance of technical activity and occupational values being intertwined.

a.reason: The paper's chief illustration that values are rooted in the work is the toxicologists, whose error-avoidance comes from seeing what goes wrong in their technique, though the firearms and narcotics descriptions also show values tied to technique.

b.basis: F92–F100, F103, F149, F167; toxicology method and error-avoidance values

a.reason: Narcotics analysts' valuing of craft, variety and autonomy as features of crystal work is one of the instances showing values rooted in technique.

b.basis: F107–F109, F111, F126–F129, F150, F167; narcotics craft and technique

a.reason: C21 ranks the nature of the work, chiefly occupational values, above status and power, so value filtering is a term in the ranking.

b.reason: The firearms account offers a technique-and-values explanation of resistance for C21 to favor over status or power, while the other two cases also inform that comparison.

a.reason: Toxicology is one of the three cases whose response pattern C21 explains by the nature of the work rather than status or power.

a.reason: Narcotics is one of the three cases making up the response pattern that C21 attributes to values and technique rather than status or power.

b.reason: Narcotics contributes a work-and-values explanation of resistance that the final account weighs more heavily than relative status or power, alongside the other occupations.
